chunks: Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Tamim al-Sarakhsi, the jurist in Sarakhs, told us, saying: Abu Lubaid Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shami told us, saying: Hashim ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Muharrami told us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq told us, from Mu'mmar, from al-Jariri, from Abu al-'Ala' ibn al-Shakhir, from Na'im ibn Qa'nab, who said:

I came to Al-Rabadha seeking Abu Dharr, and his wife said to me: He went to seek a profession. He said: Then Abu Dharr approached, leading two camels, one trailing its tail behind the other, and a waterskin was hung on the neck of each of them. I said: So I stood up and sent peace upon him, then sat down. He entered his home and spoke something to his wife, then said: Uff! Will you not add to what Allah's Messenger (peace be upon him and his Family) said: 'A woman is like a rib; if you straighten it, you break it, and in her is sufficiency.' Then he came with a plate containing something like a sand-grouse, and said: Eat, for I am fasting. Then he stood up and prayed two rak'at, then came and ate. I said: Glory be to Allah, I assumed that people would lie to me, but I did not assume that you would lie to me. He said: And what is that? I said: You told me that you are fasting, then you came and ate! He said: And I am saying it now. I fasted three days of this month, so the reward for fasting has been established for me, and it is permissible for me to break the fast during it.

key_terms.حل لي فطره: It is permissible for me to break it
key_terms.وجب لي صومه: Its fasting has become obligatory/established for me
key_terms.يمتهن: To seek a profession or livelihood

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on breaking a fast when one has vowed to fast for specific days?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Ma'ani al-Akhbar* highlights Abu Dharr al-Ghifari’s asceticism and his specific juristic practice of fasting three days of every month, a voluntary act that became obligatory upon his vow, allowing him to break it while retaining the reward. The scene underscores the scholarly tradition of distinguishing between *nadr* (vow) and *nafilah* (voluntary fast), illustrating how early companions navigated the flexibility of Sunnah practices amidst their profound piety.

en.basel-kadem: 1.	We were told by Abu Nasr, Muhammed bin Ahmad bin Tamim al-Sarakhsi, the jurist, in Sarakhs, that he said: We were told by Abu Lubaid, Muhammedbin Idrees al-Shami, that he said: We were told by Hashim bin Abdul-Aziz al-Muharrami, that he said: We were told by Abdul-Razzaq, from Mu’ammar, from al-Jareeri, from Abu’l-‘Alaa’ bin Saheer, from Na’eem bin Qa’nab, that he said:

I came to Al-Rabadha, seeking Abu Dharr, and his woman said to me: He went to seek a profession. He said: Suddenly, Abu Dharr approached whilst leading two camels, of which one had aligned to the tail of the other, and he had hanged a waterskin on the neck of each one of them. He said: Then I stood up and sent peace upon him, and then I sat down, and he entered his home and spoke something to his woman, and then said: Uff! Will you not add to what Allah’s Messenger, Allah’s blessings be upon him and his Family: «A woman is only like a rib; if you raise it, you break it, and in her is adequacy»? Then he came with a plate that had the like of a sand grouse, and he said: Eat, for I am fasting. Then he stood up and prayed two rak’at [1], and then he came and ate. He said: So I said: Glory be to Allah, as I had assumed that people would lie to me, I did not assume that you will lie to me. He said: And what is that? I said: You said to me that you are fasting, and then you came and ate. He said: And I am now saying the same. I fasted three (days) of this month, hence, its (reward for) fasting has been written to me, and it is permissible for me to break the fast during it.
